title: SIMION v. ROMANIA
summary: In the case of Simion v. Romania, the applicant, Mr. Simion, identified as a member of the Roma community, brought a complaint against the Romanian state. The case concerned the vulnerability of Roma individuals in Romania, who often face discrimination and other human rights violations, though the specific harm alleged by Mr. Simion is not detailed in the Court’s published decision. According to the available facts, Mr. Simion lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights, raising issues under several articles of the European Convention on Human Rights, including Articles 3, 4, 10, and 14, which address the prohibition of torture, prohibition of slavery, freedom of expression, and prohibition of discrimination, respectively. However, before the Court could examine the merits of his claims, Mr. Simion indicated that he no longer wished to pursue his application. As a result, on 11 September 2012, the Court struck the case out of its list, finding no special circumstances requiring further examination. While no violation was found or remedy awarded, the case highlights the procedural challenges that can arise for Roma and Traveller applicants seeking justice at the European level, reflecting broader historical difficulties in accessing effective remedies for rights violations.
